svg.title: Live-Live dual-active multicast: two groups, two independent paths, and a receiver that merges them
svg.desc: Top: one source sends the same content twice to two different group addresses, 239.10.1.1 and 239.10.1.2, over two disjoint paths through different routers and different optical transport. The receiver joins both groups and de-duplicates by RTP sequence number, so a failure on either path is invisible rather than recovered. Five requirements are listed: physically non-overlapping paths, independent RPs when sparse mode is used, one unique group per leg, receivers that can join both, and aligned clocks or sequence numbers so the two streams are comparable. Middle: the implementation layers - application-level dual send, SMPTE ST 2022-7 seamless protection switching which de-duplicates and merges by sequence number for zero-loss switching, and dual-NIC receivers. Bottom: the failure mode that destroys the whole design, two paths that are logically independent but physically shared, drawn through the same duct or the same optical transport, where one digger cuts both. A fit matrix rates market data highest, broadcast TV high, conferencing low and CCTV lowest.
svg.text: Live-Live: you do not converge faster, you make the failure irrelevant
Two groups, two paths, one picture. The receiver never waits for a protocol to notice anything.
path A: different fibre, different transport, different RP
path B: the other fibre - and it must be a different duct
loss on one leg is a loss of
the same RTP packet already arrived
The failure mode that voids the design:
two paths that are logically independent but physically shared - same duct, same optical transport, same trench.
network agnostic, receiver must be modified,
de-duplicate and merge by RTP sequence,
no protocol change at all, but it doubles the
terminal cost and the address plan
Market data (ms, zero loss) ***** Broadcast TV / live sport ***** Enterprise conferencing ** (SSM plus QoS is enough) CCTV * (recording can backfill)
The stars are not about importance. They are about what a single lost packet costs, compared with what a second path costs.
Design rule: draw the physical route, not the logical topology. A Live-Live diagram that shows two links between the same pair of boxes proves nothing -
the question is whether they enter the building through the same trench, and that fact lives with facilities, not with the network team.
